On December 16, 1919, the army of Soviet Russia (RSFSR) took Kyiv for the third time since the start of the communist revolution[89][65].The Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR) is the Ukrainian state proclaimed in 1917. By December 1919 its army - eight to ten thousand soldiers, many of them sick with typhus - was pinned near Starokostiantyniv in Volhynia: the Volunteer Army of Denikin to the south and east, the Polish army to the west, the troops of Soviet Russia to the north. Contemporaries called this position the «triangle of death»[6]. At a meeting in Nova Chortoryia on December 4-6, 1919, the head of the UNR Directory Symon Petliura and the army command decided to dissolve the regular front. The UNR Army under the command of Mykhailo Omelianovych-Pavlenko set out on a raid through the rear of the Soviet and White forces: in 180 days, from December 6, 1919 to May 6, 1920, some ten thousand soldiers marched two and a half thousand kilometres across Ukraine. This raid is known as the First Winter Campaign[6].That same winter Soviet troops occupied most of Ukraine. The dates of the cities' capture, according to the front reports: December 11, 1919 - Poltava and Kharkiv, December 16 - Kupiansk, December 24 - Luhansk, January 5, 1920 - Mariupol, February 7 - Odesa[89]. On the Right Bank the Russian occupier reached the Polish front line: Kamianets-Podilskyi, Proskuriv and Starokostiantyniv were held by the Poles[6].The UNR leadership signed an alliance with Poland and secured the support of its army in the fight against the Russian occupiers. In the spring of 1920 the armies of Poland and the UNR moved to liberate Kyiv. On May 6, 1920, Yegorov, commander of the Southwestern Front of the Soviet army, telegraphed in secret order No. 304: «Kyiv must fall to the enemy only at the cost of the heaviest losses on his part»[90]. The armies of the UNR and Poland retook Kyiv: on May 7 Polish reconnaissance units rode to the centre of the city by tram, and on May 8 ten regiments of the 3rd Polish Army entered the capital[91].The occupier gathered its forces and on June 6 broke through the Polish front south of Kyiv, at Samhorodok. On June 10 the Polish troops, having blown up the Chain and Rusanivskyi bridges, withdrew from Kyiv[91]. On June 12, 1920, Yegorov reported: «Units of the 58th Division have taken Pechersk and are entering Kyiv». The orders to cut the Kyiv - Korosten railway, issued the day before, were signed by Yegorov and Stalin[90].On October 18, 1920, an armistice took effect on the Polish-Soviet front, and the UNR Army was left to face the invader alone[91]. By November 10 it held the front with 8,968 bayonets and 3,250 sabres, with 95 guns and 687 machine guns. Against it the Soviet command moved the 12th and 14th armies, the Bashkir cavalry brigade and Kotovsky's cavalry brigade: 24,000 bayonets, 4,000 sabres, 120 guns and five armoured trains[92]. The occupation troops attacked first and thwarted the offensive being prepared in Podillia, in today's Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi oblasts. In eleven days of fighting the UNR Army lost about 13 thousand soldiers, almost all of its artillery and four armoured trains[91].On November 21, 1920, about 12 thousand UNR soldiers, together with the staff of Symon Petliura and the ministries, crossed the Zbruch River, along which ran the border with the lands ceded to Poland under the Treaty of Warsaw[91]. Mykhailo Andrusiak, a participant in the retreat, recalled: «Sadly, with bowed heads, the Cossacks laid down their arms after crossing the bridge and marched on to the West»[93].In the autumn of 1921 the soldiers of the UNR army made a last attempt to raise a general uprising against the Soviet occupiers. This raid is known as the Second Winter Campaign, and its course is known from the report of the chief of the Field Insurgent Staff, Colonel Yurii Otmarshtein, submitted to Symon Petliura. At 2 a.m. on November 4, 1921, the detachment crossed the Polish-Ukrainian border near the village of Borove: 155 officers and officials, 645 Cossacks, 32 horses, with about 56 percent of the men armed with rifles[94]. On November 7 the detachment under the overall command of Yurii Tiutiunnyk liberated the Korosten railway junction in battle and freed 600 political prisoners from the jail, but withdrew that same morning: an armoured train of the Soviet occupiers was approaching the town with guns the detachment had nothing to counter, and ammunition had to be spared. Seven officers and twelve Cossacks died in the battle[94].The detachment could go no further. Half of the infantry marched without boots and with frostbitten feet, the wagon train carried up to 80 wounded, and ammunition was replenished only with what was taken from killed and captured Russians. The staff decided to turn back, towards Poland[94]. The troops of the Russian invader blockaded the area of the UNR raid and on November 17 encircled the detachment near the village of Mali Mynky in the north of Zhytomyr Oblast. Over 400 soldiers died in the battle, 537 were taken prisoner, and more than a hundred broke out of the encirclement and crossed the Polish border on November 20[28][16]. The prisoners were taken to the village of Bazar, where 359 of them were shot[95]. The armed struggle of the regular UNR Army ended there[67]. The people will not forgive you for this!»[95]. The condemned embraced and sang «Shche ne vmerla Ukraina» - the song that seventy years later, after Ukraine declared independence in 1991, became the national anthem of Ukraine and remains so to this day[96]. To the sound of the anthem, Soviet troops shot all 359 Ukrainian prisoners near the village of Bazar[95][67]. The testimonies were gathered by a courier of the Ukrainian underground who visited Mali Mynky and Bazar immediately after the execution[95].The exact day of the execution differs between sources, ranging from November 21 to 23[95][28][16].The list of all 359 executed men, name by name, was published by Sotnyk O. Shpilinskyi in Kalisz in 1932; the list was later reprinted together with the text of the resolution[95].Historian Larysa Yakubova writes: «This execution became a tragic symbol of the Ukrainian Revolution of 1917—1921. title: Propaganda, instrument S0021
content: Propaganda A state institutional apparatus of mass ideological influence, formatting of consciousness, and cognitive control. It included specialized party structures (in particular, the agitation and propaganda departments of the Central Committee), as well as the press, the system of mass events, cinema, and literature, all fully controlled by the authorities. It was used by the aggressor to replace real history with artificial imperial-communist myths, to subject the population to total ideological indoctrination, and to deliberately cultivate a fanatical totalitarian personality type, blindly devoted to the regime and cruel toward dissenters. The propaganda machine served as the basic mechanism for legitimizing state violence and masking the policy of forced assimilation. Propagandistic Inversion of Roles and Dehumanization (1800–1864) G0009 Russian Empire S0021 Propaganda The propaganda apparatus of the Russian Empire used poetry to broadcast the logic of domination into society: the imperial historian and participant in the events V. A. Potto records that the poet A. S. Pushkin proclaimed in verse the inevitability of subjugation: «Submit, Caucasus - Yermolov is coming!»[1], while the poet V. A. Zhukovsky extolled the destruction of infrastructure by military commanders: «Scarcely at the villages - the villages blaze»[2]. January 1933 T0004 Rewriting of History C0079 Cultural Terror and the "Executed Renaissance" (1933–1938) G0010 USSR S0021 Propaganda The construction of a new Soviet-imperial historical canon to supplant the Ukrainian past: "from the late 1930s a thesis took hold in the historical scholarship of the USSR," proclaimed in the works of B. Grekov, K. Huslystyi, and F. Yastrebov, "of Kyivan Rus as the 'common cradle' of the history of the Ukrainian, Russian, and Belarusian peoples," and "in 1939 B. Grekov advanced the proposition of the ethnic unity of the 'Rus people' in the era of Kyivan Rus"[3]. This scheme displaced M. Hrushevsky's conception and denied the independence of Ukraine's history. August 1946 T0101 Censorship C0085 Postwar Ideological Terror ("Zhdanovshchina") (1946–1953) G0010 USSR S0021 Propaganda Total ideological control over art and the press, the banning of works and the vilification of writers for alleged "bourgeois nationalism." The campaign culminated in the verdict in the case of the Jewish Anti-Fascist Committee: "on July 18, 1952 the Military Collegium of the USSR Supreme Court passed death sentences on 13 people, including 5 natives of Ukraine, well-known Jewish writers and poets"[4]. August 1946 T0022 Terror C0085 Postwar Ideological Terror ("Zhdanovshchina") (1946–1953) G0010 USSR S0021 Propaganda The staging of public political persecution (attacks on Rylsky, Sosiura, Yanovsky, the campaign against "cosmopolitans"), instilling an atmosphere of fear. Its outcome was the execution of the defendants in the JAC case: "on August 12, 1952 they were all executed"[4]. January 1954 T0004 Rewriting of History C0087 The Ideological Campaign of the "300th Anniversary of Reunification" and the Transfer of Crimea (1954) G0010 USSR S0021 Propaganda A state campaign to construct a historical myth: the "Theses on the 300th Anniversary of the Reunification of Ukraine with Russia," approved by the CPSU Central Committee, declared that "by this historic act was completed the long struggle of the freedom-loving Ukrainian people against foreign enslavers for reunification with the Russian people in a single Russian state"[5] – the annexation of 1654 was retroactively rewritten as the goal and outcome of a national struggle. January 1954 T0010 Denial of a Distinct Identity C0087 The Ideological Campaign of the "300th Anniversary of Reunification" and the Transfer of Crimea (1954) G0010 USSR S0021 Propaganda The imposition of a concept of unbreakable unity instead of recognizing a distinct nation: per the Theses, "by the act of reunification the Ukrainian people consolidated its close and unbreakable historical bond with the Russian people, in whom it found a great ally, a faithful friend and defender"[5]. The celebrations and the transfer of Crimea "taking into account the commonality of the economy, territorial proximity, and close economic and cultural ties"[6] served the same frame. April 1986 T0007 Imposition of Its Own Picture of Reality C0090 Information Blockade Around the Chornobyl Disaster (1986) G0010 USSR S0021 Propaganda Creation of an artificial picture of radiological well-being and the criminal, forced marching of people into the May Day demonstrations in Kyiv under radioactive fallout to mask the catastrophe[7]. September 2004 T0006 Dehumanization C0096 Election Interference and Countering the "Orange Revolution" (2004) G0011 Russian Federation S0021 Propaganda The conduct of an aggressive information campaign in favor of "their" candidate with the direct participation of the head of the Russian state: live on three Ukrainian television channels two weeks before the vote, praise was voiced for the candidate's government - "V. Yanukovych's government achieved more: they managed to fill this growth with good quality. That is, Ukraine's economy is developing in a diversified way"[8]. In parallel, opponents were demonized with accusations of nationalism and pro-fascist views. April 2008 T0137 Disinformation C0098 Diplomatic Attack Against NATO Enlargement (2008) G0011 Russian Federation S0021 Propaganda The deliberate injection of false historical narratives into the international arena: Ukraine, according to the Russian leader, "is not a nation built in a natural manner" and "an artificial country created back in Soviet times," and its territories were supposedly gifts - "In the 1920s and 1930s Ukraine obtained territory from Russia -- that's the eastern part of the country. In 1956, the Crimean peninsula was transferred to Ukraine"[9]. From this the thesis of its possible disintegration was derived: "the country could just split apart"[9]. February 2014 T0137 Disinformation C0100 Beginning of the Russo-Ukrainian War: Armed Invasion and Occupation of Crimea (2014) G0011 Russian Federation S0021 Propaganda The official denial of Russian troops' participation during the operation – and Putin's later admission (call-in show, 17 April 2014) that the denial was a lie: "behind the backs of Crimea's self-defense forces, our servicemen, of course, stood"[10]. In the same broadcast an interlocutor congratulated him on having "honestly said that the 'little green men' are our peaceful military"[10]. April 2014 T0137 Disinformation C0101 Continuation of the Russo-Ukrainian War: Armed Aggression in the Donbas (2014–2015) G0011 Russian Federation S0021 Propaganda A massive campaign of fabricating fakes to dehumanize Ukrainians: on state television it was claimed that "Ukrainian armed forces herded city residents to the central square and publicly executed a small boy and his mother," yet "there is no evidence to support Pyshniak's claim," and the residents of Sloviansk who were interviewed did not confirm the story[11]. The same method produced the fabricated "death of a 10-year-old girl" in the Petrovskyi district of Donetsk (March 2015): BBC correspondents on the ground established that no such girl had ever existed[12]. In parallel ran an operation to conceal responsibility for the destruction of flight MH17: the Russian Ministry of Defense "made a series of self-contradictory claims blaming Ukraine, rather than Russia or Russian-led separatists, for the Boeing 777's shoot down," while a deputy defense minister publicly repeated "a fabricated claim that originated on Twitter of how a Spanish air traffic controller named Carlos saw two Ukrainian fighter jets near MH17"[13]. April 2014 T0005 Aggressor Claiming Victim Status C0101 Continuation of the Russo-Ukrainian War: Armed Aggression in the Donbas (2014–2015) G0011 Russian Federation S0021 Propaganda The exploitation of the Odesa tragedy to build a state propaganda myth and invert the roles: the actual picture, per the UN, is clashes "between supporters of unity and supporters of the federalization of Ukraine, as a result of which 48 people died," while the investigation remains incomplete and "no one has yet been held to account"[14]. The tragedy was used as moral justification for further aggression - by the same device as the "crucified boy" fake, for which "there is no evidence to support Pyshniak's claim"[11]. January 2020 T0003 Cultivation of a Logic of Superiority C0102 Ideological Preparation for the Full-Scale Invasion (2020–2021) G0011 Russian Federation S0021 Propaganda Total indoctrination of Russian society with the ideas of the philosopher I. Ilyin (so-called "white fascism") and the transformation of the "Russian World" concept into a state ideology (rashism) that justifies the metropole's cultural superiority and existential right to violence against its neighbors[15]. February 2022 T0137 Disinformation C0103 Full-Scale Invasion (from February 24, 2022) G0011 Russian Federation S0021 Propaganda Total information control and a ban on calling the invasion a war - officially it was declared a "special military operation" whose stated aims were "demilitarization and denazification"[16]. The informational cover for energy terror rested on the "response" narrative: "There is a lot of noise now about our strikes on the energy infrastructure of the neighboring country. title: Controlled Opposition, instrument S0020
content: Controlled Opposition Legal political parties, movements, or factions within the colonized society that are covertly or openly sponsored, directed, and comprehensively supported by the aggressor state. They are used as a proxy instrument for destabilization, for the procedural seizure of power from within, and for legitimizing external interference under the guise of a domestic political process. November 1917 T0133 Seizure of Power Through Election Manipulation C0071 Failure of the Political Seizure of the UNR in Kyiv (November – December 1917) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0020 Controlled Opposition An attempt to convert an electoral minority into a procedural majority at the congress. Actual support was negligible: in the Constituent Assembly elections "across the country as a whole the Bolsheviks gathered less than 24% of the votes, and in the Ukrainian gubernias only 10%"[1]. Hence the wager on capturing representative bodies: the Central Committee of the RSDLP(b) declared outright that "the transfer of government from the hands of one soviet party into the hands of another party is secured without any revolution, by a simple decision of the Soviets, by a simple re-election of deputies to the Soviets," while the All-Russian Central Executive Committee's decree of 4 December 1917 "On the right of recall of delegates" provided the mechanism for such a replacement[1][2]. December 1917 T0109 Sham Expression of Popular Will C0072 Soviet-Ukrainian War: First Invasion and the Puppet Government (December 1917 - April 1918) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0020 Controlled Opposition The staging of a sham "all-Ukrainian" congress to give the seizure of power the appearance of popular will. The real All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets in Kyiv on 17-19 December 1917 did not go the Bolsheviks' way: by the time resolutions were adopted it numbered more than 2,500 delegates, "the Bolsheviks were represented by a mere 150 delegates", and the congress backed the Central Rada[3]. The losers did not accept the outcome. Volodymyr Zatonsky - one of them, later a member of the Kharkiv government - recalled: "having gathered illegally in the trade-union building, the delegates of the congress, all of them Bolsheviks except two or three Left SRs, resolved to declare themselves the plenipotentiary Congress of Soviets of the Country, to elect a Central Executive Committee and a government of Soviet Ukraine and, having moved to Kharkiv, to enter into open struggle against the Central Rada"[4]. The new "congress" convened in a city already occupied by Russian troops: "the day before the congress of soviets opened, the Central Rada's garrison in Kharkiv had been disarmed by the troops of V. Antonov-Ovseenko, whom the Council of People's Commissars had instructed to take Ukraine by force of arms", writes historian Stanislav Kulchytsky[5]. He describes the merger thus: with the regional congress of soviets of the Donets and Kryvyi Rih basins, the newcomers "proclaimed their congress the All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets"[5]; historian Vladyslav Verstiuk writes that "an alternative congress of Soviets was hastily staged", at which "200 delegates represented 89 soviets and military-revolutionary committees", while "soviets alone in Ukraine at that moment numbered over 300"[6]. The majority of Ukraine's population stayed outside the hall - delegates from the peasants, notes historian Larysa Yakubova, "were almost absent", and the qualifier "with the participation of peasant deputies" was later scrubbed from the congress's name by Soviet historiography[7]. The assembly declared itself the All-Ukrainian Congress and proclaimed the creation of a Soviet - "supposedly truly popular" - UNR[7]. January 2012 T0113.002 Exclusion of the Native Language from Official Use C0055 The Kivalov-Kolesnichenko Law (2012) G0011 Russian Federation S0020 Controlled Opposition An attempt to legalize the marginalization of the state language in the regions: the law "On the Principles of State Language Policy" (the Kivalov-Kolesnichenko law) allowed record-keeping to be transferred to "regional languages," effectively entrenching the dominance of Russian in the Russified regions[8]. This myth outlived the centuries: as late as 1990 Solzhenitsyn reproduced it verbatim – "The return of these lands to Russia was then perceived by everyone as REUNIFICATION"[1]. January 1674 T0004 Rewriting of History C0006 Publication of the "Synopsis" (1674) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate For the ideological justification of the seizure, the Muscovite authorities received a ready-made historical canon: "the 'SYNOPSIS,' 'Synopsis, or a Brief Collection from Various Chroniclers on the Origin of the Slaveno-Rossian People' – a historical work first published by the printing house of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra (1674)"[2] – the book constructed a shared "Slaveno-Rossian" past, legitimizing Moscow's rule over Kyiv retroactively. January 1674 T0007 Imposition of Its Own Picture of Reality C0006 Publication of the "Synopsis" (1674) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The implantation of a narrative about the unbreakable bond between Kyiv and Moscow, serving the political aims of the metropole: the author sought "to give the Muscovite tsar the motivation to continue the struggle with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth" and "to ease the incorporation of the Hetmanate's elite into the Russian ruling estate"[3]. January 1674 T0010 Denial of a Distinct Identity C0006 Publication of the "Synopsis" (1674) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The deliberate dissolution of a distinct Ukrainian identity in the construct of a "single Orthodox people": the "Synopsis" subordinated Kyiv's history to the idea of a common "Slaveno-Rossian people"[2], and its political program presupposed a struggle for the "liberation… of the remaining part of the 'single Orthodox people'"[3]. Hrushevsky points out what exactly was erased: the "Synopsis" is "a brief history of Rus composed at the Pechersk Lavra, done very lifelessly and incompletely (the history of the Cossacks, the struggle against Poland, and all of Ukraine's recent history are almost entirely omitted from it)"[4]. January 1674 T0024 Justification Through Religion C0006 Publication of the "Synopsis" (1674) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The imperial historical myth was directly based on religious manipulation: expansion was justified by the concept of religious unity. The author constructed an ideologeme in order "to give the Muscovite tsar the motivation to continue the struggle with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for the liberation from Catholic rule of the remaining part of the 'single Orthodox people'"[3]. January 1685 T0100 Seizure of Religious Institutions C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The liquidation of independent jurisdiction to turn the church into an instrument of assimilation – the annexation of the Ukrainian church to the Muscovite one in 1686[5]. The Ecumenical Patriarchate later officially stated that these actions "were carried out entirely out of accord with the lawful canonical prescriptions"[6]. January 1685 T0101 Censorship C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The introduction of censorship control over Ukrainian book printing. Patriarch Joachim banned publications without his sanction and sent a reprimand for publishing books without prior permission[7][8], and in 1690 "the Council of the Russian Orthodox Church condemned the 'new Kyivan books' of Petro Mohyla, Kyrylo Stavrovetsky, Ioanykii Galiatovsky, Sylvestr Kosov, Lazar Baranovych, and others, laying on them a curse and anathema"[9]. January 1685 T0044 Destruction of Local Knowledge Systems C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The destruction of the Kyiv theological school and the declaration of its works as heresy: "All Ukrainian writings, beginning with the catechism of Petro Mohyla, were declared heretical... the council condemned virtually all the principal works of Kyivan theological scholarship"[8][7]. January 1685 T0024 Justification Through Religion C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The annexation of the metropolitanate was disguised as the protection of co-religionists: the reform was carried out "relying on the Orthodox movement against the Turkish conquerors"[7], and "Golitsyn's main project concerning Ukraine… became the reform of the Ukrainian Orthodox church, or rather – the subordination of the Kyiv metropolitanate to the Moscow patriarch"[7][8]. January 1685 T0116 Religious Assimilation C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate Immediately after the subordination began the imposition of Muscovite church standards and rites, marginalizing the local tradition. The Ecumenical Patriarchate recorded the canonical illegality of the act itself directly: "the alienation from our Throne of the Metropolitanate of Kyiv and of the Orthodox Churches of Lithuania and Poland dependent on it, as well as their attachment to the Holy Church of Moscow, were from the very beginning carried out entirely out of accord with the lawful canonical prescriptions"[6]. January 1685 T0116.003 Ban on Worship in the Native Language C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate Following the establishment of control over the metropolitanate came the gradual unification of liturgical printing and pronunciation along Muscovite models, culminating in Peter I's direct decree of 1720: church books could be printed only after being checked against Muscovite ones, "so that there be no discord or distinct dialect in them"[10]. October 1708 T0024 Justification Through Religion C0012 Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The anathema against Mazepa was proclaimed by the tsar's direct order - "be pleased to have him, for such a deed of his, publicly cursed in the cathedral church..."[8]. Part of the Ukrainian clergy refused to accept the rite: a former Lokhvytsia archpriest said during the proclamation of the anathema, "Our Mazepa is holy and will be in heaven, and your sovereign will not"[8]. The Ecumenical Patriarchate never recognized it: "the anathema was laid on Ivan Mazepa for political reasons and had no theological or canonical justification"[11]. January 1709 T0024 Justification Through Religion C0014 Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1709) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The use of the church as an instrument of punishment: the anathema was proclaimed by the tsar's direct order - "be pleased to have him, for such a deed of his, publicly cursed in the cathedral church..."[8]. No theological grounding was supplied for it, and part of the Ukrainian clergy refused to accept the rite: a former Lokhvytsia archpriest said during the proclamation of the anathema, "Our Mazepa is holy and will be in heaven, and your sovereign will not"[8]. January 1769 T0113.001 Legislative Ban on the Native Language C0044 Russification of Education and Religion (1769–1786) G0009 Russian Empire S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The mass confiscation of national educational and religious literature: "in 1769 the Holy Synod not only refused permission to print South Russian primers, but ordered the confiscation of those already in people's hands, since the primers of that time were regarded as church books"[12]. January 1769 T0116.003 Ban on Worship in the Native Language C0044 Russification of Education and Religion (1769–1786) G0009 Russian Empire S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The displacement of the local population's language from the sacred sphere: metropolitan Samuil Myslavsky's order of 26 October 1784 demanded that students and future priests practice "the reading of church books of every kind, and above all the Bible, acquiring a good and pure pronunciation" - after the Moscow model instead of the Ukrainian church tradition, under the threat of expulsion from the clerical estate[13], and in 1786 metropolitan Myslavsky prescribed to the clergy the unification of pronunciation and orthography along the Russian model[14]. January 1839 T0116.001 Forced Conversion to the Metropole's Religion C0059 Liquidation of the Greek Catholic Church (1839) G0009 Russian Empire S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The forced transfer of the Uniate faithful of the Right Bank into the empire's state church (the Holy Synod; the patriarchate in Russia was abolished until 1917) for the spiritual assimilation of the population: the Basilian monasteries – the mainstay of the Union – were liquidated throughout the empire by the mid-19th century[15].
